sec.title: Objective
sec.p: Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) remains a significant health concern, particularly among older patients. While both minimally invasive esophagectomy (MIE) and open esophagectomy (OE) are established surgical types, there is ongoing debate about their comparative long-term outcomes in older patients.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This retrospective cohort study analyzed data from 469 patients with ESCC aged over 70 years who underwent esophagectomy between May 2016 and August 2021. Patients were divided into MIE and OE groups. Overall survival (OS), disease-free survival (DFS), and postoperative complications were evaluated. Propensity score matching was performed to minimize selection bias. Complications were assessed using the Clavien-Dindo classification system.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Among 469 patients, 358 (76.33%) underwent MIE, while 111 (23.67%) underwent OE. After a median follow-up of 47.5 months, the MIE group had significantly better OS (median OS: 60.17 vs. 29.18 months, HR = 1.566, P = 0.002) and DFS (median DFS: 37.70 vs. 25.20 months, HR = 1.411, P = 0.010) compared to the OE group. After PSM, MIE remained associated with significantly improved OS (HR = 1.450, P = 0.039), while the difference in DFS was no longer significant (HR = 1.240, P = 0.201). The incidence of Clavien-Dindo grade III-IV complications was similar between groups.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: MIE is associated with better long-term survival outcomes compared to OE in older patients with ESCC, without increasing major postoperative complications. These findings support the consideration of MIE as a preferred surgical approach for older patients with ESCC to enhance survival and optimize postoperative recovery.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Esophageal cancer (EC) is one of the most prevalent malignant tumors of the digestive tract worldwide [1, 2], with esophageal adenocarcinoma being more common in regions such as Europe and the United States, while esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) predominates in East Asian countries like Japan and China [2–5]. As the global population ages, the number of older patients with EC is increasing, highlighting the importance of individualized treatment approaches for this demographic [5, 6].

Surgical intervention remains the cornerstone in the treatment of ESCC, often combined with neoadjuvant therapy prior to surgery and adjuvant therapy following the procedure [7–9]. Among surgical options, minimally invasive esophagectomy (MIE) and open esophagectomy (OE) are the two primary modalities employed in the management of ESCC. While OE has traditionally been the standard procedure, MIE has gained traction due to its potential advantages. Numerous studies have shown that MIE can result in fewer postoperative complications, which is particularly beneficial for older patients who often have reduced physiological resilience and a higher propensity for postoperative issues [10–12]. Despite these advantages, there remains considerable debate about whether MIE provides better long-term survival outcomes compared to OE [13, 14]. This aspect is crucial for older patients, who are more susceptible to postoperative complications due to their reduced physiological resilience. As the trend of an aging population continues, the focus on treatment outcomes post-OE and MIE for older patients becomes increasingly relevant.

This study focuses on the elderly demographic and aims to provide robust evidence to assist healthcare professionals in balancing surgical risks with quality of life and survival outcomes. Specifically, we addresses these concerns by comparing the long-term outcomes of MIE versus OE in older patients. The research examines OS, DFS, and postoperative complications. By identifying the most effective surgical approach for older patients with ESCC, this study seeks to inform clinical decisions and optimize patient care strategies for this growing population.

sec.title: Study design and patients
sec.p:
This retrospective cohort study was conducted using data from a prospectively collected database at Sichuan Cancer Hospital (Sichuan Cancer Hospital & Institute Esophageal Cancer Case Management Database). The study focused on patients aged over 70 years diagnosed with ESCC who underwent esophagectomy between May 2016 and August 2021. Inclusion criteria required histologically confirmed squamous cell carcinoma located in the thoracic esophagus, with no evidence of distant metastasis as determined by clinical and imaging evaluations. Patients were excluded if their tumors were non-thoracic, if they were diagnosed with non-squamous cell carcinoma, or if clinical data were incomplete. Follow-up data were collected until December 20, 2023 (Fig. 1). Patients were categorized into two groups based on the surgical approach: the MIE group and the OE group. The MIE group included patients who underwent esophagectomy using minimally invasive techniques, while the OE group consisted of those who underwent traditional open surgery. MIE is a procedure that utilizes thoracoscopic assistance to perform esophagectomy. During this minimally invasive technique, the surgeon uses specialized endoscopic equipment, inserting surgical instruments through the intercostal spaces into the thoracic cavity. With the aid of a thoracoscopic imaging system, the procedure allows for an enlarged view of the thoracic blood vessels and nerves, providing a clearer operative field for enhanced surgical precision. OE, on the other Hand, is a traditional surgical method involving a larger incision in the chest or abdominal area for direct access to the thoracic or abdominal cavity. This approach requires a 20–30 cm incision in the chest, with rib spreading to adequately expose the surgical site for the operation. The choice between MIE and OE depended on the surgical team's preoperative assessment of the complexity of the procedure and the associated risks. This decision-making process also involved discussions with patients and their families to ensure shared understanding and agreement. The primary outcomes assessed were OS and DFS. OS was defined as the time from treatment initiation to death from any cause or last follow-up, while DFS was defined as the time from treatment to disease recurrence, death, or last follow-up, whichever occurred firstly. Tumor staging was conducted according to the 8th edition TNM classification by the Union for International Cancer Control (UICC) and the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) [9]. To address this imbalance, we performed propensity score matching (PSM) between the MIE and OE groups. This statistical technique allowed us to create a more comparable cohort by balancing baseline characteristics, including tumor status, thereby providing a more accurate comparison of outcomes between the two surgical approaches. The participants included in our study are predominantly from the Sichuan province in Western China and are all of Asian descent. Given the homogeneity of the population in terms of ethnicity, with no representation of Black or White individuals, we did not perform further disaggregation of data by race or ethnicity.Fig. 1
CONSORT diagram showing patient selection. MIE, minimally invasive esophagectomy; OE, open esophagectomy

sec.title: Criterion of postoperative complications and characteristic
sec.p: Postoperative complications were categorized using the Clavien-Dindo classification system, which grades the severity of deviations from the normal postoperative course [15–17]. Body mass index (BMI) was recorded and categorized according to World Health Organization (WHO) standards to evaluate potential differences in surgical outcomes related to body composition. All adverse events were reviewed and validated by surgical team members [18, 19].

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics were summarized using descriptive statistics. Continuous variables were presented as means with standard deviations, while categorical variables were expressed as frequencies and percentages. OS and DFS were estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method, with differences between groups assessed using the log-rank test. Univariate Cox proportional hazards models were employed to evaluate potential prognostic factors for OS and DFS, including age, sex, tumor stage, and comorbidities. Significant variables (p < 0.05) identified from the univariate analysis were incorporated into a multivariate Cox regression model to determine independent risk factors. PSM was performed to adjust for potential confounders, utilizing a nearest neighbor algorithm based on variables such as age, tumor stage, KPS scores and so on. Statistical analyses were conducted using SPSS version 26.0 and RStudio version 4.3.0, with a two-sided p-value of less than 0.05 indicating statistical significance.

sec.title: Overall survival and Disease-free survival
sec.p:
After a median follow-up time of 47.5 months, the median OS for patients in the MIE group was 60.17 months (95% CI: 48.94–71.40), compared to only 29.18 months (95% CI: 23.07–35.29) for patients in the OE group. The OS rates at 1, 3, and 5 years were 86%, 55%, and 47%, respectively, for MIE group patients and 82%, 45%, and 31%, respectively, for OE group patients (HR: 1.566; 95% CI: 1.186–2.067; P = 0.002; Fig. 2A). After PSM, the median OS for patients in the MIE group was 40.20 months (95% CI: 26.63–53.77), compared to only 25.53 months (95% CI: 17.25–33.81) for patients in the OE group. The OS rates at 1, 3, and 5 years were 88%, 55%, and 42%, respectively, for MIE group patients, and 78%, 37%, and 28%, respectively, for OE group patients. Patients in the OE group continued to show significantly lower OS compared to those in the MIE group (HR: 1.549; 95% CI: 1.008–2.068; P = 0.044; Fig. 2B).Fig. 2
(A) The overall survival curve of patients with minimally invasive esophagectomy and open esophagectomy before PSM; (B) The overall survival curve of patients with minimally invasive esophagectomy and open esophagectomy after PSM; (C) The disease-free survival curve of patients with minimally invasive esophagectomy and open esophagectomy before PSM; (D) The disease-free survival curve of patients with minimally invasive esophagectomy and open esophagectomy after PSM; (E) Standardized in the subjects stratified by characteristic. MIE, minimally invasive esophagectomy; OE, open esophagectomy; SMD, standardized mean difference

The median DFS for patients in the MIE group was 37.70 months (95% CI: 27.93–47.47), whereas it was only 25.20 months (95% CI: 18.62–31.78) for patients in the OE group. The DFS rates at 1, 3, and 5 years were 75%, 49%, and 37%, respectively, for patients in the MIE group, compared to 68%, 41%, and 24%, respectively, for patients in the OE group (HR: 1.411; 95% CI: 1.083–1.839; P = 0.010; Fig. 2C). After PSM, the median DFS for patients in the MIE group was 34.60 months (95% CI: 25.55–43.65), compared to only 21.97 months (95% CI: 13.48–30.46) for patients in the OE group. The DFS rates at 1, 3, and 5 years were 78%, 49%, and 36%, respectively, for MIE group patients, and 65%, 36%, and 27%, respectively, for OE group patients. There was no significant difference in DFS between patients in the OE group and those in the MIE group (HR: 1.387; 95% CI: 0.915–2.102; P = 0.121; Fig. 2D). Figure 2E illustrates the standardized mean difference for the 1:2 PSM.

sec.title: Short-term outcomes and adverse events (Clavien-Dindo, 2009)
sec.p:
In the MIE group, 3 patients died within 30 days and 10 patients died within 90 days, while in the OE group, 4 patients died within 90 days. There was no statistically significant difference between the groups in terms of mortality within 30 and 90 days, both before and after PSM. Before PSM, the incidence of Clavien-Dindo grade III-IV complications was comparable between the MIE and OE groups, with rates of 49.44% vs. 50.45% (P = 0.726). After PSM, however, the incidence of Clavien-Dindo grade III-IV complications differed significantly between the MIE and OE groups, with rates of 45.65% and 67.27%, respectively (P = 0.011) (Table 2 and Table 3).Table 3

Further analysis revealed that, among Clavien-Dindo grade III complications, the incidence of anastomotic stenosis was higher in the MIE group (P = 0.008), but post-PSM, there was no significant difference in the incidence of anastomotic stenosis between the two groups. In terms of Clavien-Dindo grade III-V complications, the MIE group had a higher incidence of anastomotic stenosis (P = 0.006), while the OE group had a higher incidence of pulmonary infection (P = 0.038). After PSM, no other adverse events demonstrated significant differences between the two groups, except for hydrothorax, which was more prevalent in the OE group (P = 0.035) (Fig. 3).Fig. 3

sec.title: Risk factors
sec.p:
Univariate analysis revealed that OE, smoking, degree of differentiation, lymphovascular invasion, nerve invasion, complete resection, Clavien-Dindo grade, clinical, pathological differentiation grade and pathological T stage, N stage, and TNM stage were all factors influencing OS. Further multivariate analysis identified lymphovascular invasion (P < 0.001), Clavien-Dindo grade ≥ III (P = 0.030), pT4 stage (P = 0.016), pN3 stage (P = 0.001), and pTNM IV stage (P = 0.009) as significant independent factors affecting OS (Fig. 4).Fig. 4
Univariate and multivariate Cox regression analyses regarding factors affecting OS of patients. MIE, minimally invasive esophagectomy; OE, open esophagectomy

Similarly, for DFS, univariate analysis indicated that OE, smoking, degree of differentiation, lymphovascular invasion, complete resection, Clavien-Dindo grade, pathological differentiation grade, clinical T stage, pathological N stage, and TNM stage were associated with DFS. Multivariate analysis demonstrated that lymphovascular invasion (P = 0.001), incomplete resection (R1/R2, P = 0.012), Clavien-Dindo grade ≥ III (P = 0.005), and pN3 stage (P = 0.034) were significant independent factors influencing DFS (Fig. 5).Fig. 5

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Our findings demonstrate that MIE is associated with significantly improved OS compared to OE, even after adjusting for potential confounders through PSM. While DFS initially favored MIE in the unmatched cohort, this difference attenuated post-PSM, suggesting that tumor-related factors or adjuvant therapies may play a more dominant role in disease recurrence. The median OS in the MIE group was more than twice that observed in the OE group (before PSM: 60.17 vs. 29.18 months; after PSM: 40.20 vs. 25.53 months). The HR for OS before and after matching (HR = 1.566 and HR = 1.549, respectively) indicate that OE patients consistently had a higher risk of mortality compared to MIE patients. The DFS results demonstrated a similar pattern before PSM, with significantly longer DFS observed in the MIE group; however, after matching, the difference was no longer statistically significant, despite numerically longer DFS in the MIE group (before PSM: 34.60 vs. 21.97 months; after PSM: 34.60 vs. 21.97 months). Currently, many esophageal surgeons believe that, even in advanced cases, the efficacy of MIE is at least equivalent to, if not better than, that of OE.

The findings of this study align with previous research indicating that MIE offers significant advantages over OE in terms of postoperative outcomes. A 2012 study highlighted that the incidence of pulmonary infections within two weeks post-surgery was significantly lower in the MIE group (9%) compared to the OE group (29%, P = 0.005). Furthermore, during the entire hospital stay, the rate of pulmonary infections remained lower in the MIE group (12%) versus the OE group (34%, P = 0.005). This is particularly relevant for older patients who are at higher risk for respiratory complications. The length of hospital stay was also notably shorter for the MIE group, averaging 11 days compared to 14 days for the OE group (P = 0.044), suggesting that MIE may facilitate quicker recovery. In terms of quality of life, patients undergoing MIE demonstrated better recovery and functional status postoperatively [20]. However, when examining long-term survival outcomes, a 3-year survival analysis indicated that the OS rates were comparable between the two groups, with the OE group at 41.2% and the MIE group at 42.9% (P = 0.633). Similarly, DFS rates were also similar, with the OE group at 37.3% and the MIE group at 42.9% (P = 0.602) [21]. Subsequent researches suggested that while MIE may not significantly enhance survival rates compared to OE in the long term, it does offer substantial benefits in terms of postoperative recovery and quality of life [22, 23].

Moreover, a recent study published in 2024 from Japan found no significant difference in the rate of pulmonary complications between abdominal laparoscopy and laparotomy [24]. The results from the JCOG1409 study, also released in 2024, confirmed that MIE is non-inferior to OE in terms of OS and showed a significant advantage in relapse-free survival (RFS). Notably, patients undergoing MIE exhibited better pulmonary function three months post-surgery, further supporting the notion that MIE may lead to improved recovery trajectories for patients, especially in vulnerable and advanced age populations [14].

In this study, PSM was utilized to balance baseline characteristics between the MIE and OE groups, with a focus on tumor factors and complication rates. The DFS, defined as the time until recurrence or death, exhibited no significant differences between the two groups post-PSM, indicating comparable recurrence patterns. Furthermore, complication rates, including severe events, were statistically similar, suggesting a balanced overall burden of postoperative adverse events.Despite these similarities, OS was significantly better in the MIE group, with a median OS of 60.17 months compared to 29.18 months in the OE group. This discrepancy between OS and DFS outcomes warrants further investigation. One plausible explanation is the higher incidence of non-esophageal cancer-related deaths observed in the OE group. The more invasive nature of open surgery, coupled with the enhanced surgical trauma associated with OE, may lead to prolonged recovery periods and a reduced functional reserve. This is particularly critical for elderly patients over 70 years of age, who often have diminished physiological reserves. Additionally, the minimally invasive approach of MIE likely enhances postoperative recovery and treatment tolerance, especially in elderly patients, facilitating better adaptation to adjuvant therapies and potentially delaying tumor-related mortality. Unmeasured confounding factors, such as nutritional status or frailty, may disproportionately impact survival outcomes in the OE group due to the invasive nature of the procedure.

Overall, while the long-term survival rates between MIE and OE may not differ significantly, the enhanced recovery profile and reduced complication rates associated with MIE highlight its potential as a preferred surgical approach for older patients undergoing esophagectomy. The findings underscore the importance of considering not only survival outcomes but also the quality of life and postoperative recovery in surgical decision-making for this demographic.

This study has several limitations that should be acknowledged. First, as a retrospective cohort study, it is inherently subject to biases related to data collection and patient selection. Although we utilized a prospectively maintained database, the retrospective nature may introduce confounding variables that were not accounted for, potentially affecting the validity of our results. Second, while we performed propensity score matching to minimize confounding factors, there may still be unmeasured variables that could affect the long-term OS and DFS outcomes. Factors such as patients' overall health status, nutritional status, and specific comorbidities were not fully captured or controlled for in this analysis, which might influence postoperative complications and survival rates. It is worth noting that patients with more advanced tumors were more likely to undergo OE, which may partially explain the observed survival differences. While PSM was employed to address potential confounding, we acknowledge that this study remains subject to inherent selection bias, which could influence the results. Then, while we assessed postoperative complications using the Clavien-Dindo classification system, this classification primarily focuses on the severity of complications rather than their impact on quality of life. Then, for those who had passed away, the database only records whether the death was tumor-related or not, without further categorization of non-tumor-related causes. Since the enrolled patients were treated between 2016 and 2021, it is challenging to retrospectively and accurately determine specific causes of death for those no longer alive, as their family members often cannot provide precise details. At last, the heterogeneity of the preoperative treatments administered to the patients also introduced potential bias.. Future studies should consider incorporating quality of life assessments to provide a more holistic view of the patients' experiences following surgery.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In conclusion, our study demonstrates that MIE is associated with significantly improved OS and DFS compared to OE in older patients with ESCC. Although MIE may present certain complications, its overall advantages in terms of survival and postoperative recovery underscore its value as a surgical option.
